1.pericope_label: In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judea, And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

schools.summary: Barnes reasons from the ages, that the days of the preceding chapter cannot be meant since John was only six months the elder, and puts the unrecorded interval at twenty-five years or more. Ellicott notes that the kingdom of the heavens is peculiar to this evangelist and thinks the other form was preferred for readers who would hear only the visible firmament in it. Lightfoot conjectures the birthplace from a comparison of texts and dates the birth about the Passover, half a year before the nativity, so that the two conceptions and births fall on the four turning-points of the year; he also denies that the wilderness implies a hermit's life, the word meaning the country rather than the city, and supports this from rabbinic measures which distinguish a Jerusalem measure from a measure of the wilderness. Robertson treats the word for repentance as the worst translation in the New Testament, since the English means to be sorry again while the Greek means to change the mind and the conduct; the word that does mean sorrow is the one used of Judas, and he prefers the old Syriac turn ye.

Calvin fixes the date by the reigns, John being about thirty and Tiberius fifteen years in power, and draws the consequence that the office was short, the morning star giving way that the Sun of Righteousness might shine alone; he also refuses to confine the prophecy of the voice to John, since the comfort promised after the temple fell was spoken to Zechariah and Haggai and Malachi before him. Gill reads the call to repentance as aimed at particular errors, justification by works among the Pharisees and the expectation of a temporal kingdom among all.

Clarke offers two etymologies for repentance, one making the penitent understand afterwards, the other making a sinner's whole life a continued course of madness, and recalls the Latin term for a growing wise again; on the herald he supplies the imagery from Diodorus, where Semiramis had the precipices of the Zarcean mountain dug down and its hollows filled to shorten her march.

Henry dwells on the silence that preceded the ministry. Nothing is recorded of either child but the disputing with the doctors, and the heir while under age differs nothing from a servant; he turns this to two uses, that faith should look to Christ in his office rather than his person, and that young men however well qualified should be slow to put themselves forward. He adds that after Malachi there had been no prophet for above three hundred years, so that the great prophet might be the more desired.

Chrysostom asks why a herald was needed at all and gives three reasons: that Christ's dignity might appear, since he too has prophets; that the Jews might have no pretext, who complained of the one that he came neither eating nor drinking and of the other that he came eating and drinking; and that the witness should come from another mouth, since they objected afterwards that a man bearing witness of himself bears no true witness. He adds that John preached what they had never heard even from the prophets, and so gained their attention by the strangeness of it.

Augustine reads the opening phrase widely, as covering the whole space from the birth to the preaching of John rather than the childhood alone, which is what lets the return from Egypt and the twelve-year-old in the temple stand together. Gregory explains the title from the relation of voice to word: the Son is the Word of the Father, and as our speech is known by the sounding of the voice, so John is the voice by whose ministry the Father's word is heard, crying in the desert because he shows forlorn Judaea her approaching consolation. Bede grants that the same cry has sounded from the beginning through everyone who spoke by inspiration, and puts the distinction elsewhere, that John alone is called the voice because he declares as near what the others showed afar off.

debates.question: How much time does in those days cover?

positions.position: The whole space from the birth to the preaching of John, not the childhood alone
Not the days of the preceding chapter at all, an interval of twenty-five years or more having elapsed
Fixed by the reigns: John about thirty, and Tiberius fifteen years in power

debates.question: Why is John called the voice and not something more?

positions.position: Because voice stands to word as his ministry stands to the Son, the Father's word being heard through him
Because he alone declares as near what every earlier inspired speaker showed from afar

outliers.claim: Denies that the wilderness implies a hermit's life, the word meaning simply the country rather than the city, and supports it from rabbinic measures that distinguish a Jerusalem measure from a measure of the wilderness.
Calls repentance the worst translation in the New Testament, since the English word means to be sorry again while the Greek means to change the mind and the conduct.

themes: In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judea,
And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

4.pericope_label: And the same John had his raiment of camel’s hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.

schools.summary: Barnes is careful about the material, since the name misleads: this is not the fine hair from which the elegant cloth is made, nor the stuff brought from the East Indies under the same name, but the long shaggy hair woven into a coarse cheap cloth still worn by the poorer classes and by monks. He treats the locusts as common people's food, notes that among the Greeks the vilest ate such things, and takes the detail as a mark of great poverty, adding that the green kind runs about two inches and the brown about three and that they come in quantities enough to darken the sky. Ellicott makes the imitation of Elijah conscious and sets the dress against the long garments of the Pharisees and the gorgeous apparel of the scribes about the court of Herod; on the food he confirms that locusts were permitted by the law and are still eaten by the poor, salted and dried, pounded or fried in butter, tasting like shrimps, and refuses to entertain the alternative reading. Robertson quotes Plummer that John consciously took Elijah as a model, though he thinks the garb necessity rather than affectation, and asks whether such an uncouth figure would be welcome in any city pulpit today. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic cross-check, that a man who binds himself by vow from flesh is thereby forbidden the flesh of fish and of locusts alike.

Calvin alone treats the whole description as a trap for the reader. The Evangelist does not want the rough living reckoned among John's chief excellencies; having placed him in the mountains, he adds only that food and clothing suited the residence, and the point is the reverse of the ascetic one, that under a mean and contemptible garb he was held in high estimation by men of rank and splendour. Superstitious persons make righteousness consist almost entirely of outward appearances and have commonly thought abstinence of this kind the perfection of holiness; near that error is the supposition that he lived in solitude and disdained the ordinary way of living, when the only superiority of hermits and monks is that they differ from other people. He ends by complaining that ignorance has gone so far as to make an entire skin out of what was only a girdle.

Clarke notes that the coarse covering was common to the prophets and that Elijah wore it, and holds that John, designated under that prophet's name, took the same habit and the same self-denial; on the food he gives the alternative reading its hearing before rejecting it, since the word may mean either the insect or the top of a plant and many eminent commentators have preferred the plant, but he judges the insect likelier and observes that the old Saxon translator put grasshoppers. He guesses the dried insects were fried in the honey, and reports that the Gospel according to the Hebrews, as Epiphanius quotes it, adds that the taste was like manna, a sweet cake baked in oil. Wesley notices that locusts rank among clean meats but were not always to be had, so the honey served in default of them, and takes the girdle for Elijah's, in whose spirit and power John came.

debates.question: Do the locusts mean the insect or the pods of a plant?

positions.position: The insect, though many eminent commentators have preferred the plant and the old Saxon translator put grasshoppers
The insect, and it is needless, the facts being so clear, to look for the Baptist's food in the pods of the tree that bears the same name

debates.question: What does the rough dress and diet signify?

positions.position: A deliberate revival of Elijah's outward appearance, set against the garments of the Pharisees and the court scribes
A model consciously adopted, though the garb was probably necessity rather than affectation
Nothing to be reckoned among his excellencies at all; the point is that under a contemptible garb he was esteemed by men of rank

outliers.claim: Turns the description against the ascetic reading of it, holding that the only superiority of hermits and monks is that they differ from other people.
Reports from the Gospel according to the Hebrews, as Epiphanius quotes it, that the taste of the food was like manna, a sweet cake baked in oil.

themes: And the same John had his raiment of camel’s hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.

5.pericope_label: Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judea, and all the region round about Jordan, And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.

schools.summary: Lightfoot answers the question of the crowds from the calendar, that the manifestation was expected just then because Daniel's weeks were spent to the last four years, and divides the four hundred and ninety years into seven weeks to the finishing of the city and sixty-two more to the opening of the last; he also finds the phrase for the region round about in the Jerusalem Gemara and compares Pliny's usage. Barnes explains the rite from its history, that the word means first to tinge or dye and so to cleanse by applying water, that washings were already familiar among the Jews, who had for some time been administering one to Gentiles coming over to their religion, and that what was new in John was his applying it to Jews. Ellicott notices the tense, a continual succession, crowd after crowd, places the confession in the closest possible connection with the act itself, and adds that the word for confessing always implies public utterance, its plural suggesting that particular sins were named. Robertson calls it a pity that baptism should now be a matter of controversy, and takes his ground from Plummer, that it was the Baptist's office to bind them to a new life symbolized by immersion, adding the qualification himself, symbolized and not caused.

Gill lists the attractions that drew the crowds, the uncommon appearance of the man, the oddness of his dress, the austerity of his life, the weight of his doctrine, the novelty of the rite, and behind all of it a nation without a prophet for some hundreds of years that half suspected this one of being the Messiah; he also says that all is here put for many. Calvin is interested in the confession rather than the water: in the sacraments God binds himself to us as though he had given his hand-writing, and it is our part to reply, so that where the reply is absent the whole performance is an idle mockery, from which he draws his rule that adults are not to be admitted indiscriminately but only after examination.

Clarke puts the objections to immersion as questions: can any man suppose it possible to dip all the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Judaea and the country round; were women dipped as well as men, since both came, which could never have comported with safety or decency; and were they dipped in their clothes, at the risk of their lives, when it is unlikely such crowds came provided with dry raiment. Wesley presses the same objections and offers a reconstruction, that they stood in ranks along the edge of the river and John, passing before them, cast water on their heads, by which he might baptize thousands in a day, which he argues answers better to the pouring out of the Spirit that the rite prefigured.

Chrysostom sharpens two of Gill's reasons: they saw in John the great Elias, and the gift of prophecy long failed among them seemed at last revived; and the preaching was unlike anything they knew, since the old prophets had spoken of wars and the conquests of the kings of Babylon and Persia, while this man spoke of heaven and the kingdom there and the punishment of hell.

debates.question: How was the rite actually administered?

positions.position: Not by dipping: the numbers, the presence of women, and the want of dry clothing all forbid it
By water cast on the head as the people stood in ranks, which also answers better to the pouring out of the Spirit
By immersion, taken as a symbol that binds to a new life and not as a cause of anything

debates.question: Why did such crowds come out to him?

positions.position: The strangeness of the man and the rite, and a nation long without a prophet that half suspected him of being the Messiah
They saw in him the great Elias, and heard a preaching unlike the old prophets, of heaven and hell rather than of wars and empires
The manifestation was expected precisely then, Daniel's weeks being spent to the last four years

outliers.claim: Derives the rite from Jewish practice, the washing already administered to Gentile converts, so that what was new in John was his applying it to Jews.
Reads the confession as the reply owed to a God who in the sacraments binds himself as if by hand-writing, and draws from it a rule that adults be examined before admission.

themes: Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judea, and all the region round about Jordan,
And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.

7.pericope_label: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees come to his baptism, he said unto them, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:

schools.summary: Robertson observes where the rebuke happened, that John had welcomed the multitudes and then exposed the ecclesiastics in front of them, and borrows the judgment that a strong attraction here and a strong repulsion there made the two parties forget their differences for the moment; on the fruits he holds that they are not the change of heart but the acts which follow from it, and that anyone can do externally good acts while only a good man grows a crop of them. Barnes dates all the sects to about a hundred and fifty years before Christ, which is why the Old Testament knows nothing of them, and keeps to the tone of the rebuke, that no discourse could have been more appropriate or more cutting. Ellicott complains that the English is ambiguous and not happy, since it suggests fruit that prepares the way for repentance when the sense is fruit worthy of a repentance already professed by coming. Lightfoot contributes a philological correction, that the name of the greater party cannot come from the word meaning to expound, since there were women of it as well as men, the rabbis having a saying about the woman-Pharisee among the things that destroy the world.

Calvin makes the change of address a rule of teaching, that instruction is unprofitable unless the instructor asks what the season demands and what belongs to the particular hearer, and that nothing is more unequal in this respect than a constant equality; the severity follows from hypocrites being the stupidest of men, deceiving themselves along with everyone else under an outward mask of holiness.

Clarke thinks the Pharisees were in their origin very probably a pure and holy people, named from separating themselves from the pollutions of the national worship, and degenerating afterwards, keeping the rules of their institution when the spirit was gone; the Sadducees he calls the materialists and deists of the Jewish nation. Wesley defends the name John gives them as judgment rather than abuse, since Herod is called a fox and men of insidious or sensual disposition serpents and dogs and wolves and swine, which are not the random language of passion but a judicious designation by one who saw their hearts; on the fruits he distinguishes the legal repentance meant here, a thorough conviction of sin, from the evangelical, a change of heart and life.
Henry says the same more briefly, that application is the life of preaching: to others it was enough to say repent, but these needed closer dealing.

Chrysostom points out that they are not forbidden to say they are Abraham's, only to trust in it while neglecting the virtues of the soul; that men should be made out of stones he finds no stranger than Isaac coming from Sarah's womb, and the word every, he adds, cuts off all privilege of birth, so that the son of Abraham who stays fruitless suffers with the rest.

Gregory puts the diagnosis first, that men who gloried in their race would not own themselves sinners, and then reads the axe as the Redeemer himself, of haft and blade as of two natures, held by the human and cutting by the divine; on the fruits he presses the word meet hardest, holding that a man who never fell into unlawful things may use all lawful ones while one who has fallen ought to put away even lawful things so far as he used unlawful, the loss by sin measuring the gain to be sought by repentance. Augustine guards the other half of the sentence, that when Scripture speaks of wrath in God it describes him from a likeness of effects, the word belonging to the effects of his vengeance and not to any disturbance in him.

debates.question: Why does the preaching change its manner for these hearers?

positions.position: Because teaching must fit the season and the person, and hypocrisy deserves a severity that common ignorance does not
Because application is the life of preaching, and a bare call to repent was not close enough dealing for these
Because the moment required it: he had welcomed the crowds and exposed the ecclesiastics in front of them

outliers.claim: Corrects the etymology of the party's name from the fact that there were women of it as well as men, the rabbis having a saying about the woman-Pharisee among the things that destroy the world.
Guards the language about wrath in God, which describes him from a likeness of effects and belongs to the effects of his vengeance rather than to any disturbance in him.

themes: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees come to his baptism, he said unto them, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:

9.pericope_label: And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham. And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the boast was common, bound up with the belief that descent alone, or descent joined to the confession that the Lord our God is one Lord, would secure any Jew an entrance into Paradise, and that to the Jew it was all that being a Roman citizen was to a Roman and more; he finds in the saying about the stones the germ of everything afterwards taught about the calling of the Gentiles, and on the axe puts the urgency in one word, that now should rather be already, the present of an act no longer future, partial judgments having been the pruning of branches while this leaves only preservation or destruction. Barnes draws the comparison out, that God could more easily make worthy children of Abraham from these stones than make subjects of the kingdom out of the proud and hypocritical, and makes the axe a figure of the preaching itself, a searching kind of address in which men are tried by their lives and not their birth. Robertson says the words touched the tender spot, their ecclesiastical pride, and gets the urgency from the grammar, since the verb means the axe lies at the root already, there and ready for use. Lightfoot identifies the opening phrase as a Jerusalem idiom found everywhere in the Talmud, and takes the axe for the Romans, adding that the Talmud applies the same prophetic words to the destruction of the city.

Gill describes the inward use of the boast, their pleasing themselves with the thought and repeating it as proof that they stood in favour and had a right to every privilege; on the axe he will not have it mean the gospel, though he grants that this cut down their self-confidence, and takes it for the judgment of God, laid not to some branches only but to the root of every privilege they had, and so to the covenant itself. Calvin describes the psychology the rebuke assumes, that until hypocrites are hard pressed they sleep in their sins or amuse themselves, and when summoned cast about for some covering to interpose between themselves and God, the covenant serving as a shield for a bad conscience; the axe he makes the purging of the Church, and states a sequence he thinks general, that grace is never shown for the saving of the godly until judgment has first appeared for the destroying of the world.

Wesley calls the presumption almost incredible and quotes a saying of theirs, that Abraham sits near the gates of hell and suffers no Israelite to go down into it. Clarke makes the axe political, since the prophets had long represented doomed nations as forests marked for felling and here the nation is the tree and the Romans the axe; he reads the words as leaving not a moment to spare and describes a woodman who, having marked his tree, lays the axe at its root and strips off his outer garment so his blows may fall with full force.

debates.question: What is the axe laid to the root?

positions.position: The judgment of God, laid to the root of every privilege and so to the covenant itself
The Romans, the nation being the tree marked for felling
The preaching itself, a searching address in which men are tried by their lives and not their birth
The purging of the Church, judgment on the world going before grace to the godly

outliers.claim: Measures the presumption by a saying of their own, that Abraham sits near the gates of hell and suffers no Israelite to go down into it.
Finds in the saying about the stones the germ of everything afterwards taught about the calling of the Gentiles.

themes: And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

11.pericope_label: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire: Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

schools.summary: Barnes describes the sandal, a piece of wood or leather bound on by thongs, and says loosing and binding them was the work of the lowest servants, whose business it was to carry their master's about. Lightfoot supplies the legal form: a servant could be bought by service, and the service sealing the purchase was this very one, loosening the buyer's shoe and carrying his things to the bath, so the sentence means whose servant I am not worthy to be. Ellicott adds that mightier looks two ways, to saving and to punishing, so the Coming One is at once Deliverer and Judge; on the fan he grants the imagery was familiar from the prophets and marks what is new, that the Coming One is himself the agent, that the older picture stopped at the scattering while this goes on to the burning, and that the fire is called unquenched. Robertson reports two constructions of the promised baptism, Spirit and fire as a double baptism under one preposition, or fire in the sense of separation like the fan that follows, and notices that the verb for cleansing the floor means to sweep it clean from side to side.

Calvin explains why the disclaimer was necessary: the people were in danger of transferring to John the honour due to Christ, and rather than let silence confirm them he declared outright that he was not the Christ; he also explains the order of the two verses, grace first and judgment second, so that hypocrites who despised the author of salvation might dread him as an avenger. Gill offers the gospel and then prefers the judgment shortly to fall on the unbelieving nation, and describes the implement from the rabbis, three hand-shaped instruments with more or fewer teeth.

Clarke calls the office of the shoes the work of the vilest slaves among Jews and Greeks and Romans alike, citing Arrian and the Babylonian Talmud; on the fan he is particular, that the Romans are God's fan here as they were his axe a moment ago, the floor is Judaea, and the wheat gathered into the garner he sees in the Christians sent to Pella before the city fell. Wesley reads the fire as love, not to be quenched by many waters, and points to its visible appearance at Pentecost.

Chrysostom answers from the sequence: while the sacrifice was unoffered and the Spirit had not descended on the water there was no forgiveness to be had, so John's work was to bring a people who never perceived their sin to a sense of it. He denies that any comparison is intended in the word mightier, since the speaker puts himself below the rank of a servant; and he notes that the words are not that he shall give the Holy Ghost but that he shall baptize in him, a metaphor for abundance, drawing from the ease of the outward rite that under the faith the will alone justifies.

Gregory answers from the office why a baptism that forgave nothing was administered at all: John could not remit sin, but the forerunner must go before in this as in his birth; and he puts the threshing at the end, after the threshing of this life in which the grain groans under the chaff, when the fan of the last judgment will so divide them that no chaff passes into the granary and no grain falls into the fire. Augustine answers that John baptized because Christ was to be baptized by him, and asked why Christ was not then the only one, replies that some would have argued John's baptism the greater, since Christ alone had the merit to receive it.

debates.question: What is the fan, and when does the threshing happen?

positions.position: The judgment shortly to fall on the unbelieving nation
The Romans, the floor being Judaea and the garnered wheat the Christians who withdrew before the city fell
The last judgment, after the threshing of this life is over
The coming of the Messiah, who sweeps the floor clean from side to side

debates.question: Why did John baptize at all, if his baptism forgave nothing?

positions.position: To keep the office of forerunner, his baptism preceding as his birth did
Because no forgiveness was yet possible, and his work was to give a people a sense of their sin
Because Christ was to be baptized by him, and others with him lest his baptism be thought the greater

outliers.claim: Supplies the legal form behind the saying about the shoes, since a servant could be bought by precisely this service, so that the sentence means whose servant I am not worthy to be.
Identifies the garnered wheat with the Christians who withdrew to Pella before Jerusalem fell, making the whole figure a prophecy of the Roman war.

themes: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

13.pericope_label: Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him. But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me? And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him.

schools.summary: Ellicott will not pretend the question is easy: the Sinless One had no sin to confess, yet his righteousness was human and therefore capable of increase, as he increased in wisdom and stature, so that height upon height of holiness rose before him, after which, he says with reverence, the Lord hungered and thirsted. He also sets out the difficulty about John's prior knowledge instead of solving it, since this narrative seems to imply it while the fourth Gospel asserts he did not know him until after the baptism, and supposes that look and tone and silence rather than any communication spoke of a stainless life; on the reply he stresses the word now, since hereafter John would be the receiver and not the giver, and notes that it becometh us covers both men. Robertson reads the meeting as the first between the two, the Baptist recognising the Coming One before the promised sign appears, and says the explanation satisfied John, since otherwise the Messiah would have seemed to hold aloof from his forerunner. Barnes observes that no precept of the older law required this, so what was given was the sanction of an example, and adds that the occasion served for God to declare publicly whom he had appointed.

Calvin keeps to the plainest ground, that Christ received the same baptism as we do to assure believers they are grafted into his body, and hears in the reply a deliberate setting aside of rank; on John's knowledge he insists that the Baptist acknowledged him not as a distinguished prophet, as he says many foolishly dream, but as the Son of God, yet finds him mistaken all the same, since the refusal was plausible only so long as he forgot that the baptism was asked for the sake of others. Gill holds that John knew him already, not through kinship nor previous acquaintance but by immediate revelation, so that the descent of the Spirit confirmed a knowledge already given rather than supplying it, and reckons the interval at about six months.

Clarke renders the phrase as every righteous ordinance and supports it from Justin Martyr, that Christ was circumcised and kept the other ordinances not for his own justification but to fulfil the dispensation committed to him. Wesley divides the duty, the one to receive the rite and the other to administer it.

Henry marks the break. From childhood until now the Lord had lain hid in Galilee as if buried alive, and after a long dark night the Sun of righteousness rises; and he begins not at Jerusalem but where John was baptizing, because there had gathered the people who waited for the consolation of Israel.

Chrysostom argues from the Law: Christ was to end it after his baptism, and came at this age so that, having kept it, he could not be charged with cancelling what he had been unable to observe; against the scandal of the thing he says that the humiliation is where the exaltation shines, since the one amazement is that being God he would be made man, and the rest follows in course of reason.

Augustine turns the act around: he was baptized not that he might be cleansed but that the water might be cleansed for us, and from the hour he was dipped in it he has washed our sins away in it; and lest anyone wonder that a corporeal substance should reach the soul, he answers that water is penetrating by nature and made more so by the blessing.

debates.question: Why should a sinless man come to a baptism of repentance?

positions.position: Because his righteousness was human and so capable of increase, and holiness still unattained rose before him
To keep the Law at the proper age before putting an end to it, so that he could not be charged with cancelling what he could not observe
Not that he might be cleansed but that the water might be cleansed for us
To assure believers that they are grafted into his body by the same baptism

debates.question: Did John already know who he was?

positions.position: Yes, by immediate revelation, the descent of the Spirit confirming rather than supplying it
The narratives conflict, this one implying knowledge and the fourth Gospel denying it; the impression came from look and tone rather than from any communication
Yes, and as the Son of God, though he was mistaken in refusing, having forgotten that the baptism was asked for others

outliers.claim: Marks the break in the narrative, the Lord having lain hid in Galilee as if buried alive until the Sun of righteousness rises after a long dark night.
Supports the phrase about fulfilling righteousness from Justin Martyr, that Christ kept the ordinances not for his own justification but to fulfil the dispensation committed to him.

themes: Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.
But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?
And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him.

16.pericope_label: And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that the Lord and the Baptist alone perceived it and says there is not the slightest ground for supposing a manifestation to anyone else; on the closing words he notes that the tense points to a definite act rather than a continuing acceptance, and that the term for a beloved son is the one the Greek Old Testament uses where the English has only. Barnes takes the opposite view of the voice, that it was probably heard by everyone present and was a public declaration, and reads the last clause as a constant delight. Lightfoot observes that no voice is found sent from heaven between the giving of the law and this baptism, takes what the Jews relate of the daughter of the voice partly for fables and partly for something worse, and asks why prophecy should have been withdrawn if heavenly oracles were to continue. Robertson takes the good pleasure as a timeless aorist.

Calvin divides the benefit: since the Evangelists say John saw the Spirit, the sight was chiefly for his sake, though Christ also, so far as he was man, gained from it a further certainty of his calling; he allows a real parting of the visible sky so that John could see beyond the planets, but refuses to inquire further, since it is enough that it was a symbol of the divine presence. Gill reads the rabbinic stories about heavenly voices as a device to make such voices seem common.

Clarke reads the grammar so that the heavens were opened to John and John saw the Spirit lighting on Jesus, and rejects as far-fetched the view that the likeness of a dove refers to a hovering motion rather than the shape of the bird, counting the passage no mean proof of the doctrine of the Trinity. Wesley holds precisely the reading Clarke rejects, a glorious appearance of fire, perhaps in the shape of a dove, descending with a hovering motion until it rested on him; on the voice he names the parts, the Father speaking, the Son spoken to, the Spirit descending, and asks what praise could stand beside the Father's delight.

Chrysostom asks not about the appearance but why there was one: in the beginnings of spiritual things visible signs are given for those who can form no idea of what has no body. He adds the older history the bird recalls, that in the flood a dove brought the olive branch and tidings of rest, so now a dove points out the liberator and brings, for a branch, the adoption of the human race.

Augustine is careful about what such a sending means: the Spirit is said to be sent when an appearance is created for the time in which he may be visibly shown, and it is this visible operation, not any change in his invisible substance, that the word describes. On the voice he marks what is new, that the Father taught by Moses and the prophets in type that the Son should come and now shows him already come; and he offers an analogy, that in their own substance the Three are One without interval of place or time, but in a speaker's mouth they are three separate words that cannot be uttered at once, and in writing each fills its own place, by which one may understand how a Trinity indivisible in itself can be shown dividedly in a visible creation.

debates.question: Who saw and heard what happened?

positions.position: The Lord and the Baptist only; there is no ground for supposing a manifestation to anyone else
The voice, at least, was probably heard by everyone present, and was a public declaration
Chiefly John, since the Evangelists say he saw the Spirit, though Christ as man gained a further certainty from it

debates.question: Does the likeness of a dove name a shape or a motion?

positions.position: A shape; the hovering-motion reading is far-fetched and the terms of the text will not bear it
A motion; an appearance of fire descending with a hovering movement until it rested on him

outliers.claim: Offers the analogy of three spoken words, which cannot be uttered at once and in writing each fill their own place, to show how a Trinity indivisible in itself may be displayed dividedly in a visible creation.
Notes that no voice is found sent from heaven between the giving of the law and this baptism, and asks why prophecy should have been withdrawn if heavenly oracles were to continue.

themes: And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
